jRP1ddYFbJg.label: Jayden Daniels, Thursday
bullets: Owned the end of the Giants game again: "I'm the one that controls that huddle." He said not to put it on Dan Quinn or offensive coordinator David Blough.
Uses his dad's 24-hour rule: one day to feel sorry for yourself, then move on. With a Monday game, he said it stretched to 48.
On the 5-0 49ers: cut the pre-snap penalties, communicate, and be ready for a hostile crowd on the road.
Teams keep sending zero blitzes at him, and he says he and Blough have answers for it.
Best detail: Marcus Mariota told him every great quarterback goes through adversity.

OstrFV__f4A.label: Dan Quinn, Wednesday
bullets: "We've turned the page from Sunday. A lot of hard truths to go around." Asked whether anyone stood up in front of the team and took responsibility: "Yep. My responsibility. Point blank, period."
The last play has been "dissected, discussed, and corrected internally," and that's where it stays. He'll make tweaks to game management, down to where he stands and how he communicates.
Trey Amos, Nick Cross and Jeremy McNichols get full practice loads. Stefon Diggs and Percy Butler sat out Wednesday, and he's hopeful they get reps later in the week.
On Jayden: "very stoic," "definitely back," and "a really resilient guy."
Pre-snap penalties: more officials at practice and more cadence work. On the 49ers, he called Kyle Shanahan "exceptional, especially on the early downs."

Ab3HFGGV5no.label: David Blough, Friday
bullets: Took the last play on himself: "I'm the one with the last line of communication to the quarterback. It falls on me." Next time, there's a different plan.
Why that play: with the weather and the field, "we just wanted to help the kick."
"It's a scar that we will all wear, but we go forward."
Third downs were 4 of 12 against the Giants, too often third and 8. The fix is better first and second downs.
Three pre-snap penalties in a five-play stretch pushed them backward in the red zone. Sam Cosmi has been "absolutely fantastic," an anchor for the line.

dKjzcMYAXUg.label: Daronte Jones, Friday
bullets: On the second-half fades: the message is "reset," calm down and play the technique that worked in the first half. He put part of it on his own calls: "it's my job to eliminate that stress."
The softer fourth-quarter coverage wasn't meant as a prevent defense: same technique, same alignment, still competing.
On Mike Sainristil's penalty that wiped out an interception: "don't put those type of decisions in the hands of officials." He also called him steady, "a positive shining light."
Trey Amos's availability is still being worked out, and he'll get "some grace" coming back.

On the 49ers: get Brock Purdy off his spot and his efficiency goes up, not down. "Motion causes emotion," and "it's not how they line up, it's how they wind up." Also: Deatrich Wise "looks like Robocop" in his padding.

THId-3isyiQ.label: Command Center, 49ers preview
bullets: Santana Moss, Fred Smoot and Logan Paulson on Jayden's return: 103 rushing yards and two touchdowns, and the brace didn't slow him down.
The 49ers' defense might be the fastest laterally in the league, and they expect more blitzes after what the Giants did.

Their offense: Brock Purdy is rolling, Mike Evans is the new weapon, Christian McCaffrey gets used like a slot receiver, and Deebo Samuel is out. Sonny Styles against George Kittle might be the biggest game of his rookie career.
Our defense has 7 takeaways (tied for third-most) and a +5 turnover margin (second-best in the league).
Fred Smoot on the NFC East standings: they look like his grandma's bingo card. "All we need is one."

9vNYdXNERcs.label: Dan Quinn, Saturday
bullets: Four players are ruled out and won't travel to San Francisco: Bill Croskey-Merritt, Javontae Jean-Baptiste, Charles Omenihu and Marcus Mariota. Everyone else is on the plane, with final decisions on Monday.

Bill reinjured the same groin. With him out, Quinn called Jeremy McNichols "one of our most professional" players after a very good week, and likes Rachaad White's cutting ability plus Austin Ekeler's explosiveness as a receiver.

He saw the page turn at Thursday's practice, when the team's fight and execution finally synced up. It was the fewest penalties of any practice week, with very few plays needing a redo, and Saturday was all about the red zone.

On the 49ers: they rarely give up big plays because the second and third tacklers arrive fast, so the offense has to take explosives when they're there. "You don't chase them, but you do have to hunt them."

With two edge rushers out, rookie Joshua Josephs gets more snaps, and Quinn now sees him bending around the edge to go with his length. On Jayden: more mature, more fight, and a bigger leadership presence this season.

ABlimFSKL70.label: Dan Quinn, Tuesday
bullets: Terry McLaurin needs surgery and will miss the rest of the season. Quinn talked with him on the flight home and again after testing, and said he's "gutted for him" as a captain and one of the team's real leaders.

No other injury news yet, including Treylon Burks, because imaging is still going on after the late return; updates come Monday. To replace McLaurin, Quinn will spread his roles around: Van Jefferson had an excellent camp, and Burks and Dyami Brown bring over-the-top speed, but contested catches were Terry's superpower.

The bye is a self-scout, and Quinn expects tweaks, not a new system or new plays. The plan is a more streamlined menu of things they can hang their hat on, and he said "100%" players who don't fix the details will lose reps.

He called the offensive line's night below the standard in both pass and run blocking, and he's still hunting for the right combination. The defense is giving up too many explosive passes, so the fix starts pre-snap: disguise, communication and faster calls.

On Jayden's fourth-down throwaway, Quinn told him on the spot that even with a flag down you still take your shot. Fun detail: half the press corps asked questions from airplanes, and Quinn still sees "a golden opportunity this year in our division."

pOJXHtMqe2M.label: Command Center, bye week
bullets: With Terry McLaurin out for the year with a torn patellar tendon, the crew sees receiver by committee: Stefon Diggs takes a bigger load, Treylon Burks, Dyami Brown and Antonio Williams rotate in, and Chig Okonkwo becomes more of a focal point.

Fred Smoot's silver lining: it's "harder to study six of y'all than it is to study one," especially with Jayden spreading the ball around. The flip side is a mental test, since guys moving up the depth chart have to be ready for bigger roles.

Film room on Chig's 29-yard catch against the 49ers (he went a perfect 7 for 7 for 69 yards): a short motion pins the corner, Burks clears out deep, Chig lines up inside for a clean release, and a John Bates block helps Jayden get to the edge on the bootleg.

The bye is for finding an identity. Next up: the Eagles on Sunday Night Football, then the Rams, a Giants rematch and the Bengals on Monday night, so three prime-time games in November. Santana Moss only cares about the Eagles, Smoot wants the Rams as a measuring stick, and Logan says the Jaguars are the better test.

Brian Mitchell rewatched his first return touchdown, from the 1991 opener, and the crew made a Hall of Fame push for him and London Fletcher. Their message: "Voters, we know you watch Command Center."

-hN2w7z1MYo.label: Dan Quinn, Monday
bullets: Injury news: Treylon Burks is working back into practice today, and Marcus Mariota and Charles Omenihu are back too. Javon Kinlaw's knee isn't coming along as fast as hoped, so he stays in rehab, and Bill Croskey-Merritt's groin won't be rushed this time. Austin Ekeler and Rachaad White carry the backfield in the meantime.

Why Steve Wilks joined the staff: Quinn and Daronte Jones had talked about adding a veteran voice since training camp, and Wilks kept coming up. He helps build the defensive game plan early in the week. On offense, David Blough's pass game coordinator role already covers that job.

The self-scout covered all three phases separately, then Quinn did one for the whole team. The big theme is playing a full game instead of a good half: "I haven't loved all four quarters together." Some coverages get a set number of tries to work, or they're gone.

On Kurt Warner's point that Jayden could be more aggressive into tight windows, Quinn called it fair in certain games but loves his ball placement, especially on deep shots. With Terry McLaurin out, Stefon Diggs' workload stays about the same, and Antonio Williams is the one in line for more targets.

The run game fix is more strategy than personnel: use all 11 guys, including Jayden carrying out fakes, and finish blocks downfield so a two-yard run becomes four. Human moment: Quinn said Trey Amos came back from his reinjury with "no flinch in this competitor." Now it's all Eagles, three straight conference games, two in the division.

9gzPiYzRwd4.label: Dan Quinn, Wednesday
bullets: Injury news: Jer'Zhan "Johnny" Newton's 21-day practice window is open after he got hurt in the first preseason game, and Quinn is pumped to have him back. Stefon Diggs sat Wednesday but goes full Thursday, and resting him early in the week will be more common than not. No update on Bill Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw looks unlikely for Sunday.

How the bye self-scout worked: each coordinator met with players one on one to hear what they see on the field, the R&D staff flagged where the team ranks high and low, and Quinn did the team-wide scout himself, watching every game start to finish in order. Red zone pass defense was one example. That chapter closed Monday night, and now it's all Eagles.

On first-time coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones: on-the-job training is hard but works. Blough had to handle quarterback injuries and Jones had to stop the explosive plays, and Quinn likes that both lean on the staff instead of shutting the door and figuring it out alone.

He expects "two angry teams willing to fight to the last snap" on Sunday night. He won't overthink Philly's injuries, and he isn't pleased with the pass rush, so he spent time with that group syncing up blitz, rush and coverage. The 49ers game summed up the problem: three straight three-and-outs to finish, after a first half the team basically skipped.

Austin Ekeler has learned the system and is ready for a bigger workload. Laremy Tunsil is healing on schedule, with his next checkup "weeks away, not months away." Human moment: Quinn said this team's adversity has built constructive energy with no finger-pointing, and his favorite finish of the year was Seattle, while the close losses to the Eagles and Giants were his least favorite.

VsSYE1CCSVg.label: Jayden Daniels, Wednesday
bullets: On Terry McLaurin's season-ending injury: on the field it's next man up, but in the locker room it's a real blow because of Terry's energy, presence and leadership. Jayden said it's going to "sting for a little bit," and the rest of them have to hold it down while he's gone.

His big self-scout takeaway is urgency in and out of the huddle. Faster subs and play calls give him more time at the line to read what the defense is showing, and he says he has to get better at painting the picture for everyone once the call comes in.

He's comfortable in the offense but sees room to grow, mostly in over-communication so the line, tight ends, receivers and backs all understand the whole concept, not just their own route. David Blough is very receptive and constantly asks what he likes and doesn't, thanks to three years of rapport even though it's Blough's first year calling plays.

On Kurt Warner's point that he could have been more aggressive downfield against the 49ers: he didn't play a perfect game and is always his own biggest critic, win or lose. On the stumbles pulling away from center, he said "it's all on me."

He has never loved the spotlight, and it doesn't change his routine. Sunday night against the Eagles carries more weight for sure, but the division is still there to chase, one day at a time. He also praised Austin Ekeler as sudden and decisive out of the backfield, and said this team fights to the end but hasn't put a complete game together yet.

opjsMYkuUJs.label: David Blough, Thursday
bullets: With Terry McLaurin out, rookie Antonio Williams gets more targets and snaps. Blough likes how he's refining his route running, details and splits, and says the thing you can't deny is that the ball just finds him. Chig Okonkwo is playing at a high level on first and second down, and the plan is to get him in space for all 60 minutes.

The bye week deep dive stayed inside the offensive staff, and some changes are already showing up in practice: simpler personnel names and groupings so guys get out of the huddle faster. The biggest hangup so far has been third and fourth down, plus self-inflicted stuff like illegal shifts and formations that put them behind the sticks.

On Jayden: Blough sees his own job as being "the best caddy in the world" for him. Working out of a huddle with longer play calls is still fairly new for Jayden even in year three, his comfort is growing, and Blough expects a big jump by game 10 and again by games 14 and 17.

Austin Ekeler is a true professional. In London he was specifically ready for 15 to 20 plays out of a 100-play game plan, and he has added more every week since. Van Jefferson's word is trust: everyone in the building knows he'll be where he's supposed to be if he's needed Sunday night.

He leans on veterans like Marcus Mariota and Laremy Tunsil to shape the system, because "a good idea knows no rank." The offense's personality is that it's never out of a fight, but it has never strung together 60 good minutes. Fun detail: asked if he understands the illegal shift rule, he said yes, the team just hasn't been clean enough.

1S-4FUz8TWk.label: Daronte Jones, Thursday
bullets: His one-word grade for the pass rush so far: inconsistent. There are stretches where it's explosive and moving the quarterback off his spot, and others where it disappears. The self-scout fix is peeling back some of the layers so players can line up, get their feet set and just play fast.

Washington blitzes more than anyone except the Vikings, so why isn't it working? Jones says it's execution of assignments and rush paths, plus winning one-on-ones, since free runners are rare. The whole front is now meeting together so everyone sees the protection the same way, with no individual rushes.

Facing a backup quarterback in Philly doesn't change the prep. The Eagles still have an experienced staff, the ball comes out quick, and they came out on fire against Dallas. He won't guess at their injuries, including Saquon Barkley's: "we can't kick our own butt."

Nobody is putting the pass defense on Trey Amos. Jones wants his expectations tempered since he isn't back to his old form yet, but just being out there was huge for his confidence. Dorance Armstrong is still finding his groove after missing camp and working on his conditioning, and Jones knows how valuable he is to the rush.

Jones didn't bring any assistants with him, so the staff rehearses each install on one another before presenting it to players, and the self-scout stayed in-house, with coaches swapping run and pass film for fresh eyes. Human moment: the 49ers week message was "second half" over and over, and then the halves flipped, though he loved that the guys kept battling.

H4ttiqU9QbU.label: Command Center, Eagles preview
bullets: Tanner McKee starts for Philly, and Logan calls him a really good backup with real limits: take away his first read, make him pat the ball, and send pressure while the Eagles' reshuffled offensive line is still figuring out its combinations. The crew wants to stop the run and make McKee throw it 50 times, especially with Saquon Barkley getting rubbed down on the sideline against Dallas.

On offense, Logan wants Jayden more aggressive, taking the shots he passed up in San Francisco, since the run game will be more selective without Bill Croskey-Merritt. Santana Moss says don't be predictable on first down: screens, draws and pushing it downfield to keep the Eagles guessing.

Without Terry McLaurin, Moss sees a whole room filling the void: Stefon Diggs as the leader, Antonio Williams as the rising star, Treylon Burks finally getting his moment, and Van Jefferson as the steady veteran. Moss also calls this a tone-setter for the second half of the season rather than a must-win.

Film room on the week one game: Diggs beating Cooper DeJean one on one, Rachaad White wide open on a crossing route once Philly's zone got stretched, Sonny Styles' first career sack on a Daronte Jones first-down pressure, and Nick Cross blowing up a bubble screen before it started.

Fun stuff: Fred Smoot's riddle, "What's an eagle with no wings? That's chicken," sparked a full debate over whether chickens can fly. Smoot also remembered the 2001 team turning its season around after the bye by just running the ball and playing defense, and Shawn Springs picked Jayden as the player who has to rise under the lights.

HRlFb6AAedA.label: Dan Quinn, Friday
bullets: Injury news: Javon Kinlaw is out Sunday night and will be reassessed next week, and he's the only player ruled out so far. Charles Omenihu is back after an Achilles and then a groin bothered him, which Quinn called a big deal for the pass rush. He loves Omenihu's football awareness and arm length, and said "he's a better run defender than I was expecting based on his size."

Steve Wilks will be on the sideline this week as another set of eyes, sending information back through the iPad. His heavy lifting is the Monday through Wednesday game plan, and he'll join for games when his schedule allows. Asked why not a full-time hire, Quinn said it's common in the NFL and that he used Ben McAdoo and Brian Schottenheimer the same way in Atlanta and Dallas.

On simplifying things: it's both the play language and each player's job. Fewer "if they do this, we do this" layers so guys play fast and decisive, since chasing a certain look can cost you aggressiveness. Without play-calling duties, Quinn sees his game-day job as feeding coordinators what he sees and clearing out clutter. For the illegal shifts, practice now drills taking a beat so everyone gets set.

On his first-time coordinators: there's no "here's your diploma" moment after six games. Nobody is happy with the record, but he likes the practices and communication, and now the team has to execute for a whole game. The reset idea came from good first halves and bad second halves, so at practice he'll mark off a bad flag and make the next play harder on purpose.

Player notes: Antonio Williams settling at one receiver spot should mean more snaps, Daron Payne's strength inside does dirty work that never shows up in a stat line, and he likes Chris Paul in pass protection and Brandon Coleman's speed to the second level, minus the false starts. Fun one: his hat has been forward lately because the sun was in his face in San Francisco. He normally wears it backward.

F40Nrs0gv8A.label: Dan Quinn, Monday
bullets: Injury news: Jeremy McNichols has a midfoot injury, and Quinn said "I'm concerned it's serious." More scans are coming and he'll update it Wednesday. With Bill Croskey-Merritt on IR until Arizona week, the team will look at its practice squad backs and talk about bringing someone in if McNichols can't go against the Rams.

The false starts are on everybody. The long cadence was meant to draw the Eagles offside, but four flags going the wrong way is not good enough, and two in a row turned a third and one into a third and 11 on the slow start. Asked how many times he'll keep repeating it, Quinn said "as many as it effing takes."

The pass rush looked the way he pictured when they signed these guys: more coordinated and connected, with Charles Omenihu in the middle of it and Dorance Armstrong and Odafe Oweh felt all night. Trey Amos is past the limited snaps of San Francisco and back to looking like himself, Nick Cross communicated well from the nickel spot, and Frankie Luvu showed his most speed and blitzing since the opener.

On offense, the timing was a fraction off for the first quarter and a half before the team found its rhythm in the two-minute drive before the half. Quinn likes Jayden's decisions on ball location and how much better he's gotten at sliding and getting down on scrambles. One explosive he singled out: a 25-yard comeback to Treylon Burks that sets up a double move later. Luke McCaffrey's kickoff and punt returns flipped the field.

Best moment: after Drew Stevens missed from 55, Quinn sent him right back out for 56 because it was as calm a night, wind-wise, as he can remember at home, and he didn't want his kicker doubting himself. He admits he held his breath. He also loved Jayden pulling teammates together on the bench late in the first quarter, since it's better when that message doesn't come from the head coach.

9S0GraePptU.label: Dan Quinn, Wednesday
bullets: Injury news: Quinn opened by saying the team has lost three tough guys, likely for the season, and the questions made clear the interior line is now without Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne. Kinlaw had hoped to play through his injury, but the evaluations from the team's doctors and outside opinions never changed. The good news: running back Robert Henry Jr. is back on the team.

Next up inside: Quinn liked what he saw from the interior against Philly with Charles Omenihu back, and Shy Tuttle will get leaned on more at nose tackle because he has quickness and wins with leverage, alongside Tim Settle. Jer'Zhan Newton had a good first week back, and the goal is to stack another one. Quinn is very optimistic and says Newton is in crazy shape.

Rams scouting: Matthew Stafford struggles under pressure but rarely gets blitzed, because Sean McVay's system leans on bigger personnel and play action and Stafford knows where to go with it. Against Davante Adams and an offense that flips between three tight ends and three receivers, the message is eyes and details, since against good route runners this is not the time to guess.

The four-man rush was better coordinated against the Eagles, with nobody too high or too low, and the blitz package can now play anything from zero to cover two to fire zone behind it. Add the blitz to a rush that collapses the pocket and "now you're cooking." Dorance Armstrong looked closest to his pre-knee-injury self, Quinn sat next to him in the defensive meeting to tell him so, and the staff likes moving him inside on long yardage with Omenihu and Odafe Oweh for more speed.

On the penalties, the players are now part of the fix and helped pick which cadences to use this week, with every team and walkthrough rep run the same way. Rachaad White's long run on the final drive came from a sideline check that everyone knew to make. Human moment: Quinn said the feeling of a winning locker room is "not for sale," it has to be earned by everybody, and he sees the chase in the standings as energy his team can use.

3D9t9mF499c.label: Jayden Daniels, Wednesday
bullets: The bye-week communication fixes showed up against the Eagles. The chain from the staff to David Blough on personnel, from Blough to Jayden, and from Jayden to the huddle was smoother, and he said "all that was crisp."

On scrambling, it's all about picking his spots: check it down or throw it away instead of taking a short sack, and once he breaks contain, find a guy downfield or take the 15 yards and get down. He said he bought into the offseason changes right away after talks with Blough, Dan Quinn and Adam Peters about how he could grow as a quarterback and a leader.

With the running back room banged up, Jayden says everybody gets paid to do their job. Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler and whoever is up this week have to trust the line and tight ends, and it's the offensive staff's job to fit the game plan to whoever is healthy.

After his sideline talk flipped the Eagles game, the goal is to carry that urgency all week and stop shooting themselves in the foot, because "nobody's bigger than the standard that we have set." He loves Treylon Burks' growing confidence after a rough start to his career, saying his long stride eats up ground so fast that you have to get the ball up early. Antonio Williams earned his trust with a high football IQ and that big second-and-nine catch late.

Fun detail: Jayden and Matthew Stafford have a good relationship and train at the same spot in Southern California. He admires how much control Stafford has spinning the football and hopes to get there one day. As for the Rams' front, he said you can't treat those guys like anybody else, and the rest of their defensive line is really good too.

rwIME4kkp10.label: Daronte Jones, Thursday
bullets: Rams scouting: Matthew Stafford gets the ball out so fast, and Sean McVay's protection scheme is built so blitzes often don't pay off. Jones says you can't speed Stafford up because he's already sped up, so every pressure has to be calculated, sometimes just the illusion of one. He called it "more of a chess match" than blitzing for the sake of blitzing.

Puka Nacua is the headache. The Rams line him up everywhere, jet him across the formation and run him through the line, so having one corner follow him around would leave that corner fitting the run like a linebacker. The answer is what Jones calls premium awareness: every player who could be in coverage has to know where Nacua is before the snap, a lesson from Jaxon Smith-Njigba getting loose late in the Seattle game.

The back end is steadier now. Trey Amos healthy on the outside lets the defense play both two-corner and three-corner looks, and Nick Cross back means more big nickel, with Cross down by the box or deep in the zones. Frankie Luvu overcommunicates with the front and the back, and his veteran presence calms guys down when an offense gets rolling.

With the interior line thinned out, Charles Omenihu and Byron Cowart held up at tackle. Omenihu brought pass rush from the inside and length that helped set edges, and Jones joked he can touch the floor from where he stands. Cowart is a stout vet who is strong at the point of attack. Steve Wilks on the sideline took things off Jones' plate so he could focus on the next call. The two go way back but had never worked together.

Human detail: K'Lavon Chaisson surprised the staff with his energy. On days he's out or taking a vet day, you can feel the practice energy drop, because "he brings the juice." Sonny Styles is getting more comfortable in his coverage drops, and his long frame changes the throwing lanes. The Eagles game was a snapshot of what the pass rush can be with Chaisson, Dorance Armstrong and Odafe Oweh, and now the goal is stacking practices and games until it's the standard.

02aIth0I4kY.label: Command Center, Rams preview
bullets: Eagles win highlights: Rasul Douglas' interception, Dorance Armstrong's strip sack, Treylon Burks' 53-yard catch, Stefon Diggs' fifth touchdown of the season (he leads the team), and Chig Okonkwo's one-handed grab in traffic. The receivers also honored the injured Terry McLaurin with a touchdown celebration, which Santana Moss said showed how much he means to that room.

Who took the next step: Moss picked Burks, who made the most of his first start since getting a second chance. Fred Smoot picked Trey Amos, who he thinks will prove he's the No. 1 corner, and Logan Paulsen picked Tim Settle for holding down the middle with Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw out. Paulsen also loved how aggressive Jayden was from the pocket, like firing to Chig under pressure, a playmaking side he says hasn't shown up in a couple of years.

The defense numbers: five sacks against Philly and 10 takeaways in the last five games, tied for the best turnover margin in the NFL at plus seven. Smoot's message to fans was "let grandma cook," since players are finally learning Daronte Jones' A-gap and B-gap pressure and tighter coverage. In the film room, Paulsen showed the controlled chaos confusing a young Eagles center, Smoot called Deatrich Wise Jr. a lumberjack, and Amik Robertson got love as a pitbull in run fits.

London Fletcher's keys for the Rams: Stafford, the reigning MVP, already has eight interceptions, matching his total from all of last season, so change the picture before and after the snap and get him off his spot. Linebackers have to take double teams off the defensive tackles against the Rams' two running backs, and with no Davante Adams, expect more targets for tight end Tyler Higbee on in-breaking routes. Puka Nacua had 24 targets in one game a couple of weeks ago, so the volume is coming.

Fun stuff: Fletcher called in from his home trophy room and invited Smoot to come "take a whiff of what greatness looks like," just not to stay long. John Riggins' No. 44 gets retired at halftime Sunday, making him the seventh player in franchise history with that honor. Paulsen said Riggins was his mom's favorite player growing up, and Moss admitted he mostly knew Riggins as a radio host and didn't know he was a Super Bowl MVP.

VkolONAgjTM.label: Dan Quinn, Friday
bullets: Injury calls come tonight, when the staff huddles up on a couple of guys. One player who hasn't practiced all week could still go, though Quinn admitted that's harder and being able to do the walkthroughs buys some grace. Dyami Brown hurt his calf Thursday, with no word yet on how bad, which thins a receiver room where only two of the guys at practice had caught a pass from Jayden this season. Quinn's answer: they've caught plenty in practice, and this is exactly why everybody on the roster gets reps.

Depth guys are getting their shot. Quinn thanked Van Jefferson for trusting the team and coming back on the practice squad even with chances to play elsewhere, and expects him to play well. Robert Henry Jr., who has never played in an NFL game, spent early mornings this week getting caught up and told the staff he'll be ready, and Quinn likes what he's seen from Devin Neal and Craig Reynolds too. Jaden Bradley could be in line for snaps after months as the featured player on the scout team, where Quinn bets all those practice targets speed up a young receiver's growth.

Rams scouting: the offensive linemen said communication has to be even sharper this week, and Quinn agreed, since the Rams' front has quickness inside and out and can blitz, move around or win rushing four. On Myles Garrett, Quinn said it's hard to simulate that kind of explosiveness, called him bigger than you think, and said he's a complete player in the run game, not just a pass rusher. On the other side, giving premium attention to the Rams' top targets can mean a post safety helping in man coverage, a reroute in a roll coverage, or a double team on a critical down.

Special teams got some love. Teams are now planning for Tyler Owens on punt coverage, and Quinn called him and Percy Butler a true duo who earn that extra attention with their speed and physicality. He liked the return units staying on their blocks against the Eagles, noting "there's not a stat for that." Jordan Magee and Kain Medrano stood out too: Quinn says his linebackers can run like safeties, which is exactly the speed today's kickoffs demand.

Human side: with a lot of first-year assistants this year, Quinn said he was more intentional than ever in the offseason, with offsite staff summits and filmed installs he could give feedback on, because he was once a young coach that other people poured into. Developing coaches is "not just add water," and sometimes it means hard truths, but he credits the staff's closeness through the early-season adversity with setting an example for the players. He opened by honoring John Riggins, whose jersey gets retired Sunday, saying Riggo is what identity looks like.

BXFILf6n-mY.label: Dan Quinn, Monday
bullets: Injury news on a short week: Amik Robertson's ankle responded well overnight, and Quinn is optimistic heading into Tuesday and Wednesday. Treylon Burks, who missed the Rams game, got some work in Saturday and gets more Tuesday, which Quinn called the big day for judging his readiness, though he's more optimistic about this one. Lucas Patrick leaving Sunday's game also cost the offensive line some continuity.

The Giants on Thursday night: Quinn says he's seen too many crazy seasons to make one-game declarations, but "man, we need this win this week," against the division leaders at their place. Sunday's loss changes nothing at the trade deadline, either. Calls and conversations are normal this time of year, with no shift because of the result.

On fans criticizing offensive coordinator David Blough for the end-of-game calls, Quinn defended him as an "incredibly competitive and talented guy" and said people don't see what goes into each call. He also owned that the team has to find a way to score at the end, and that execution is on players and coaches alike. He was frustrated by two false starts, from the center and the left tackle, after a full week of work on cadences, and noted neither came on a silent count.

The run game wasn't up to standard, but Quinn's fix isn't just handing it off more. Back-to-back three-and-outs in the third quarter meant fewer cracks at it, so it comes down to converting third downs and extending drives. That also ties into Myles Garrett: the line mostly faced him one-on-one because quick, three-step throws don't get chip help, and staying out of a straight dropback game is part of keeping a player like that from wrecking things.

On Jayden's throws leaning short this year, Quinn said it's a mix of coverage and design, and getting Burks back would add another downfield threat. With Terry McLaurin, Burks and Dyami Brown all hurt after receivers came out of camp healthy, every injury now triggers an audit of practice, recovery and even fueling. He liked a play-action design where Antonio Williams broke inside and back out, and on Stefon Diggs having one catch until late, Quinn said he loves Diggs' fire and that he's always at the front of the staff's thinking.

bullets: Lineup news: Nick Allegretti is back at center against the Giants. He had been working mostly at guard while banged up, and Quinn said moving him on a Tuesday is much easier than a shift at the end of the week because Nick gets to run the calls and communication all week. With Allegretti and Matt Gulbin both having plenty of reps together, Quinn says the line shuffling doesn't throw Jayden off the way it might have early in the year.

The short week is squeezed: Tuesday doubled as a Wednesday and Thursday practice, Wednesday is the Friday routine, then they hit the road. Fixing the run game starts with third downs, since extending drives means more at bats for it, plus a game plan built around where the Giants are vulnerable. Quinn called it dialing in, not wholesale changes.

Giants scouting: Quinn says you can feel John Harbaugh's identity on that team, built on time of possession and a run game it stays committed to, with a pass defense that's among the league's best. They blitzed a ton in the last meeting, so the offense needs answers that turn five, six or seven rushers into big plays. On defense, J.J. McCarthy uses his legs to extend plays and can rip deep throws, so containment is part of the plan.

Accountability check: Quinn wasn't pleased with the two false starts Sunday and said repeats of the same thing would get under his skin. He likes the fixes the line made, but if it keeps happening, that's when personnel changes come. The red zone got extra reps for a second straight week, with separate plans against man and zone so the decisions happen fast. He also praised Daronte Jones' defense for better tackling and fewer explosive plays allowed since the second half of the 49ers game.

Human side: asked to compare this stretch to his past, Quinn thanked the reporter for saying he'd been around "some" and not a really long time, like other people do. He still won't call Thursday a must-win, but "everybody in this building" knows how badly they need it. On trade deadline day, he said it never even came up with the team. The focus was all game plan.

bullets: The theme was process. Asked what the up-and-down last few weeks taught him, Jayden said he won't change who he is or his routine based on the outcome. He's had receivers like Treylon Burks and Van Jefferson rotating in, and three different centers this season, and his answer to all of it was the same: stay consistent within himself and he can play with anybody.

On why the team hasn't put four full quarters together yet, Jayden was blunt that you want to hit the ground rolling from day one and "that's just not what the reality is right now." Guys have been in and out of the lineup, himself included, so they're playing the cards they were dealt.

On offensive coordinator David Blough, Jayden said they're far ahead of where they were in OTAs, but Blough is a first-time coordinator going through growing pains. The collaboration is real: plays Jayden doesn't like during the week get taken out, and ones he loves get called. His bottom line is that if all 11 guys go the same direction, they have a chance.

Giants prep: they blitzed Washington around 60 percent of the time last meeting, and Jayden says the fix is having answers, from checks he can make himself to protection adjustments built into the play. He called the Giants a team full of athletic players who love to get into the mix and create mismatches. In the red zone, windows are tighter, so routes and timing have to be precise and receivers have to win contested catches.

Fun moments: asked why the tight ends other than Chig Okonkwo have been quiet as receivers, Jayden laughed it off and said you'll have to ask Blough. He praised Van Jefferson's competitive edge and tough catches against the Rams. On trade deadline day, the locker room isn't talking about it: "we let the front office do what they do."
